extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students in probability / Markov chains and researchers needing reference proofs and techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of coupling methods, periodicity, tail σ-fields, Harris chains, recurrence/transience, stationary measures, convergence theorems, and ergodic theorems for Markov chains (countable and general state space). Includes examples (random walks, GI/G/1), constructions, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, build two sequences X_n and Y_n on the same probability space to conclude that X_n converges in distribution by showing P(X_n ≠ Y_n) → 0, or more generally, that for some metric ρ, ρ(X_n, Y_n) → 0 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coupling often proceeds by running two copies independently until they meet and then forcing them to move together. The exposition gives explicit couplings (independent copies and a modified q which makes coordinates move together after hitting the diagonal) and explains that bounding P(X_n ≠ Y_n) gives bounds on total variation distance, e.g., ||p^n(x,·) − π(·)|| ≤ 2 P(T > n). Useful anti-pattern: failing to construct a coupling that preserves marginals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence to stationary distribution via coupling (total variation bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using two copies (one started at x, one in stationary π) and the hitting time T of the diagonal, one has ||p^n(x,·) − π(·)|| ≤ 2 P(T > n) → 0 under irreducibility/recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs product chain, shows recurrence of product chain (stationary distribution π⊗π), defines T the time of first intersection, and uses Markov property to equate distributions post-intersection. This yields an explicit probabilistic bound on total variation distance in terms of the coupling time tail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite state irreducible aperiodic mixing (existence of power with strictly positive entries)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is finite and p is irreducible and aperiodic, then there exists m so that p^m(x,y) > 0 for all x,y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a structural criterion used to prove exponential convergence to equilibrium. Reduction to the strictly positive case by considering a power of p is suggested; once p^m has all positive entries, one can obtain geometric ergodicity (P(T > n) ≤ C r^n for some r<1,C<∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submultiplicative contraction α_n and exponential decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Define α_n = sup_{i,j} (1/2) Σ_k |p^n(i,k) − p^n(j,k)|. Then α_{m+n} ≤ α_m α_n, and if α_m < 1 for some m, α_n → 0 exponentially fast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation via coupling: α_n is twice the worst-case total variation between n-step distributions. Use subadditivity (multiplicativity here) and Lemma 2.7.1 to get exponential rates. Useful check: find m with α_m<1 to infer geometric convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong law for additive functionals of Markov chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose p is irreducible with stationary distribution π and f has finite π-expectation. Decompose path at returns to x, define i.i.d. blocks V^f_k of summed f over cycles; then time averages (1/n) Σ_{m=1}^n f(X_m) → Σ_y f(y) π(y) almost surely (for any initial µ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (i) show cycle sums V^f_k are i.i.d. with finite expectation; (ii) relate number of cycles up to time n to expected cycle length; (iii) control maximal block contributions. This gives ergodic averages for Markov chains and is a constructive approach using regeneration at returns to a state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central limit theorem for additive functionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Under irreducibility, stationarity π, E_π f = 0, and finite second moment of cycle sums, the centered normalized sum n^{-1/2} Σ_{m=1}^n f(X_m) converges in distribution to a Gaussian (c χ) under any initial distribution µ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the random index CLT applied to sums over i.i.d. cycles and shows negligible contribution of the last incomplete cycle. Requirements: finite second moments for block sums and zero mean under π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclic decomposition and periodicity (Lemma 5.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an irreducible recurrent chain with period d, there exist residues r_y ∈ {0,...,d−1} so that the set K_y = {n≥1: p^n(x,y)>0} equals {n: n ≡ r_y (mod d)}. The state space partitions into S_0,...,S_{d−1} (cyclic decomposition) with transition constraints reflecting periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition is essentially unique up to rotation; it identifies irreducible classes for p^d (which are aperiodic). Use to analyze limiting behavior when d>1 and to define which times transitions are possible between classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence theorem in the periodic case (Theorem 5.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is irreducible, has stationary distribution π, and all states have period d, then for x∈S_0 and y∈S_r, lim_{m→∞} p^{md+r}(x,y) = π(y) d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: mass spreads over the cyclic classes and limits occur only along subsequences congruent to r (mod d). The theorem reduces to applying the aperiodic convergence theorem to p^d on each cyclic class and uses dominated convergence to identify the limit as π(y) d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail σ-field for periodic recurrent chains (Theorem 5.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is irreducible, recurrent, and all states have period d, then the tail σ-field T equals σ({X_0 ∈ S_r} : 0≤r<d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: for such chains any tail event is determined by which cyclic class the chain started in. Proof proceeds by regeneration arguments, Hewitt–Savage 0-1 law on cycles, and reduction to the single-class (aperiodic) case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space-time harmonic functions ↔ tail variables (Theorem 5.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounded Z ∈ T correspond 1-1 to bounded space-time harmonic functions h : S × {0,1,...} → R so that h(X_n,n) is a martingale; specifically h(x,n) = E_x[Y_n] for Y_n with Z = lim h(X_n,n) and Z = lim_{n→∞} h(X_n,n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical representation of tail-measurable bounded random variables via martingales of space-time harmonic functions; conversely, every bounded space-time martingale limit is tail-measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling constructions for simple random walk (coordinate coupling)
rubrics_metrics.description: For d-dimensional simple random walk, couple two walks by using the same coordinate index at each step; once a coordinate agrees, move that coordinate identically thereafter. Such a coupling ensures P(X_n ≠ Y_n) → 0 in recurrent dimensions and identifies cyclic decomposition (parity classes L_0, L_1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: choose coordinate i_n uniformly and signs; make the same sign choice if walks already agree in that coordinate. Use to show tail σ-field reduces to parity class and to demonstrate hitting/coupling behavior in various dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornstein's coupling (big jumps in parallel)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an irreducible aperiodic random walk on Z with step distribution f, modify coupling by taking large jumps in parallel (same realization) and small jumps independently; this yields P(X_n ≠ Y_n) → 0 and so trivial tail σ-field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose M so that truncated distribution f_M is irreducible/aperiodic; let big jumps (|Z_n|>M) be coupled identically, small jumps independent. Useful technique when direct synchronous coupling is not available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harris chain definition (general state-space criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markov chain X_n is a Harris chain if there exist sets A,B ∈ S, ε>0, a function q with q(x,y) ≥ ε for x∈A,y∈B, and a probability measure ρ concentrated on B such that (i) for τ_A = inf{n≥0: X_n ∈ A}, P_z(τ_A < ∞) > 0 for all z ∈ S; (ii) if x ∈ A and C ⊂ B then p(x,C) ≥ ∫_C q(x,y) ρ(dy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a framework for general-state-space chains that admits regeneration-type arguments. The conditions ensure a uniform minorization on A→B transitions and that A is visited with positive probability from anywhere. Examples: countable chains with a common accessible atom, continuous-density chains with local positivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct augmented chain with atom α to manufacture returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Given (A,B,q,ρ) as in Harris condition, define ¯S = S ∪ {α} and transition ¯p by: for x∉A, ¯p(x,C)=p(x,C), ¯p(x,{α})=ε; for x∈A, ¯p(x,C)=p(x,C)−ε ρ(C); and ¯p(α,D)=∫ ρ(dx) ¯p(x,D). Define v leaving S mass unchanged and returning α according to ρ. Then v ¯p = ¯p and ¯p v = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction creates an artificial atom α so that ¯X_n visits α with positive probability; it is used to transfer regenerative and stationary-measure arguments from the atomic setting to general Harris chains. The lemmas relating p,¯p and v are essential bookkeeping steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer relations between original and augmented chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Key identities: v ¯p = ¯p and ¯p v = p; if ¯f = v f (i.e., ¯f(x)=f(x) for x∈S and ¯f(α)=∫ f dρ), then E_µ f(X_n) = E_µ ¯f(¯X_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equalities permit deriving limit theorems and stationary properties for X_n from results for ¯X_n (the augmented chain). They also justify regenerative-sum representations of stationary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence/transience via the augmented chain atom
rubrics_metrics.description: Define R = inf{n ≥ 1 : ¯X_n = α}. The augmented chain is recurrent iff P_α(R < ∞) = 1; otherwise it is transient. Equivalently, recurrence corresponds to infinitely many returns to α a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the general dichotomy to hitting behavior of the artificial atom α. Use R_k (k-th return) and geometric renewal arguments (P_α(R_k < ∞) = P_α(R<∞)^k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of σ-finite stationary measure in recurrent Harris chains
rubrics_metrics.description: If ¯X_n is recurrent, define ¯µ(C) = E_α[Σ_{n=0}^{R−1} 1{¯X_n ∈ C}]. Then ¯µ is a σ-finite stationary measure for ¯p, and µ = ¯µ v is a stationary measure for p (and ¯µ ≪ λ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the regenerative-cycle construction of a stationary measure: integrate occupation measure over one cycle between visits to α. Show ¯µ¯p = ¯µ and derive µ p = µ via ¯µ v p = ¯µ v. Check σ-finiteness using sets where ¯p^k(x,α) ≥ δ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of stationary measure up to scaling in recurrent Harris chains
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is recurrent and ν is a σ-finite stationary measure, then ν = ν(α) µ, where µ is the stationary measure constructed from returns to α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof passes to ¯ν = ν ¯p (so ¯ν(α) < ∞), then compares ¯ν and ¯µ via return-time identities (argument mirrors countable-state uniqueness proofs). This gives uniqueness (up to multiplicative constant) of σ-finite stationary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence theorem for aperiodic recurrent Harris chains (Theorem 5.8.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_n be an aperiodic recurrent Harris chain with stationary distribution π. If P_x(R < ∞) = 1 for the starting state x, then ||p^n(x,·) − π(·)||_{TV} → 0 as n → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use augmented chain ¯X_n and the regeneration atom α; construct independent copies starting at x and at stationarity and couple via their visits to α to obtain τ (joint hitting time), then bound total variation by P(τ > n). The hypothesis P_x(R<∞)=1 holds π-a.e. by prior lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI/G/1 queue recurrence/stationarity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For the GI/G/1 waiting-time recursion W_n = (W_{n−1} + ξ_n)^+ with ξ_n = η_{n−1} − ζ_n, if E ξ_n < 0 then a stationary distribution exists; if E ξ_n > 0 the system is transient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation via random walk S_n = Σ ξ_i: W_n relates to the reflected random walk and its supremum M. Use renewal/random-walk maxima techniques to deduce recurrence/transience and existence of stationary law. Exercises guide through equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference-of-exponential lemma (useful in queue computations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ≥ 0, Y ≥ 0 independent, and P(X > x) = e^{−λ x} (Exp(λ)), then P(X − Y > x) = a e^{−λ x} where a = P(X − Y > 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via integrating the exponential tail against distribution of Y: P(X − Y > x) = ∫ P(X > x + y) dF_Y(y) = e^{−λ x} ∫ e^{−λ y} dF_Y(y) = e^{−λ x} P(X − Y > 0). Useful to compute ladder height distributions in GI/G/1 examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pollaczek–Khintchine context and transform formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For Poisson arrivals (ζ exponential) with E ζ > E η, ladder-height and supremum transforms lead to the Pollaczek–Khintchine formula: E e^{−s M} = (1 − α E η) s / (s − α + α B(s)), where B(s)=E e^{−s η_n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formula is given as a result of ladder-height analysis and renewal-type decompositions; derivation requires careful decomposition of maxima and use of transforms. Use when arrivals are Poisson or service times exponential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ergodic theorem for stationary sequences (Chapter 6 opening)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is a stationary sequence and E|f(X_0)| < ∞, then the time averages (1/n) Σ_{m=0}^{n−1} f(X_m) converge almost surely as n→∞; if the underlying measure-preserving transformation is ergodic, the limit equals E f(X_0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework: represent stationary sequence via a measure-preserving map ϕ on (Ω,F,P) and X_n = X ∘ ϕ^n. Ergodicity means invariant σ-field is trivial. Examples: i.i.d. sequences (Kolmogorov 0-1 law gives ergodicity), Markov chains with irreducibility and full-support stationary π are ergodic (discussion continues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ergodicity criteria — i.i.d. and Markov chains
rubrics_metrics.description: I.i.d. sequences: ergodic because invariant σ-field ⊂ tail σ-field and Kolmogorov's 0-1 law makes tail trivial. For Markov chains on countable S with stationary π positive on all states, decomposition into irreducible closed sets shows ergodicity iff chain is irreducible (otherwise invariant sets are the closed irreducible components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checking ergodicity reduces to checking triviality of invariant events; for Markov chains, use irreducibility and recurrence properties. The textbook begins an argument using the Markov property and invariant indicator functions to deduce constancy.
